title: Log-squared query complexity of fixed-dimensional Tarski fixed points
formal: For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(k\ge1\), let \(Q(n,k)\) be the minimum worst-case number of deterministic adaptive value queries needed to find a fixed point of an unknown monotone function \(f:[n]^k\to[n]^k\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Is \[\forall k\ge1\ \exists C_k>0\ \forall n\ge2:\quad Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2?\] A query at \(x\in[n]^k\) reveals the entire vector \(f(x)\) at cost one. Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. The constant \(C_k\) may depend on \(k\) but not on \(n\) or \(f\); no polynomial bound on its dependence on \(k\) is required.
definitions: The grid \([n]^k\) consists of all integer vectors with \(k\) coordinates in \([n]\). Its order is coordinatewise: \(x\le y\) means \(x_i\le y_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). The oracle promise is that \(x\le y\) implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). A fixed point is a vector \(x\) with exact equality \(f(x)=x\); any fixed point is an acceptable output, with no least or greatest requirement. For given \(n,k\), a deterministic oracle decision tree is finite. Each internal node names a query vector and has branches indexed by possible returned vectors; the next query depends only on \(n,k\) and the preceding transcript. Each leaf outputs a vector that is a fixed point for every promised oracle consistent with that leaf. Paths inconsistent with every promised oracle impose no correctness requirement. The tree’s cost is the maximum number of internal nodes on the path followed by any promised oracle. \(Q(n,k)\) is the minimum such cost over all correct trees, with a separate tree allowed for each pair \(n,k\). Thus no uniform or efficient construction of the optimal trees is built into the target. The only access to the unknown function is through the counted queries; no table, circuit, auxiliary advice about \(f\), randomness or quantum query is provided. Reading or manipulating a returned vector and other finite internal computation do not add query cost. Monotonicity on this finite complete lattice guarantees existence of a fixed point. Every logarithm in the bound has base two.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed bound or its negation. A positive answer must establish correct decision trees with the stated worst-case query bound for every fixed dimension and every side length. A negative answer must show that there exists one fixed \(k\) such that, for every \(M>0\), some \(n\ge2\) satisfies \(Q(n,k)>M(1+\log_2 n)^2\). A logarithmic exponent that increases with \(k\), or a lower bound whose contradiction requires \(k\) to increase with \(n\), does not settle the assertion. The target places no bound on internal computation time; a query-efficient result need not yield a polynomial-time algorithm for succinctly encoded functions.
why: Fixed points of monotone maps underpin equilibrium existence and program semantics. The oracle problem isolates how much information about a function is needed to find one. A dimension-independent logarithmic exponent would reveal a strong structural limit on that information requirement, even with dimension-dependent constants and unrestricted internal computation.

importance.reason: A broad oracle-complexity question about monotone fixed points, with a surprising low-dimensional pattern and connections to equilibrium search. It distinguishes intrinsic information requirements from implementation time.

status_note: The March 2026 primary preprint explicitly leaves a squared-logarithm bound with a dimension-dependent multiplier unresolved for general fixed dimensions, while proving it in dimension four. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the full target; the September quantum lower bound concerns a compatible parameter dependence. These status checks do not certify every cited proof independently.

context_blocks.text: Etessami’s 2022 seminar question asks for improved bounds for finding any Tarski fixed point, distinguishing black-box queries from a succinct circuit input. This card retains the previously selected concrete question of a squared logarithm for every fixed dimension. It does not claim that such a query bound alone supplies a time-efficient solution of the broader circuit problem.

Chen, Li and Yannakakis prove an \(O(\log_2^2 n)\) query upper bound in dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Together with previous bounds this gives \(\Theta(\log_2^2 n)\) in dimensions two, three and four. Their general upper bound is \(O((\log_2 n)^{\lceil(k-1)/3\rceil+1})\), with constants permitted to depend on \(k\).

Brânzei, Phillips and Recker prove a lower bound \(\Omega(k(\log_2 n)^2/\log_2 k)\) for \(n,k\ge2\), even for randomized algorithms measured by expected queries with success probability at least \(9/10\). It also applies to the deterministic worst-case model, but for each fixed \(k\) its extra dimension factor is only a constant.

The conclusion of the March 2026 paper explicitly leaves a generic squared-logarithm bound with dimension-dependent multiplier as a possibility. It also states that its new query algorithm is not time-efficient, which is compatible with this card’s unrestricted internal-computation model.

A September 2026 preprint of Li, Ma, Yang and Zhao gives an \(\Omega(k\log_2 n)\) lower bound for quantum queries. This newer result does not contradict the squared-logarithm target at any fixed dimension. Only its primary abstract and model summary were used in this bounded later-work check.

sentences: The input is oracle access to a monotone function on a finite grid of fixed dimension.
Each query reveals one full function value, and any exact fixed point is acceptable.
The question asks whether the worst-case deterministic query count is bounded by a squared logarithm of side length in every fixed dimension.
A March 2026 result establishes that bound in dimension four while leaving the general fixed-dimension question unresolved.
Resolving the target would clarify the information needed for monotone fixed-point search without also requiring fast internal computation.
